item.title: REVIEW: Qalo SL-1 vs. Garmin Cirqa: How these minimalist wearables compare
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Qalo SL-1 vs. Garmin Cirqa: How these minimalist wearables compare Both screenless bands cost about $200 and work without a subscription, but their specs are pretty different. Garmin and Qalo both launched screenless fitness bands just 10 weeks apart this year — and also priced them four cents apart at about $200 each. Garmin announced the Cirqa on July 21, and Qalo followed on September 29 with the SL-1. Neither of the bands has a display or requires a paid membership to work, separating them from Whoop, whose bands come with a membership starting at $199 per year. Looking at their respective spec sheets, Qalo claims the longer battery life while Garmin lists the deeper water rating, more activity types and more training metrics. The Garmin wearable also has an optional paid software tier that Qalo doesn't. We've tested both in depth: our Garmin Cirqa review scored it 7.4 out of 10, while our Qalo SL-1 review gave it 6.8. Qalo sells the SL-1 for $199.95 with a black silicone strap and a charging dock. Extra straps will set you back $34.95 apiece. No subscription is required to use the band, and the companion app is free. Garmin's press release says the $199.99 Cirqa tracks its features without the need for a subscription. That said, there is an optional tier called Connect+, which costs $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year. Cirqa's manual lists things like AI-generated insights, nutrition logging, Live Activity Stats, training guidance and a performance dashboard among the features that need the subscription. It also says that guided workouts require a subscription, and that some activities may too. Both bands are eligible for HSA and FSA spending. Qalo lists the SL-1 at 18 grams and 10.5mm thick but doesn't say whether that weight includes the strap. Garmin's Cirqa is 14.8 grams without the strap and 20.7 total grams with the smaller wristband. The SL-1 is worn on the wrist, about an inch above the wrist bone, on a silicone strap with a woven one sold separately. Meanwhile, the Cirqa sports a fabric hook-and-loop band that comes in two wrist sizes and can also be worn on the upper arm with a long arm band. Garmin offers four colors, and the Cirqa has one side button, a multicolor status LED and vibration alerts for alarms and a Find My Band feature. Qalo's support pages describe only a charging status light. Garmin has rated the Cirqa at 5 ATM, which its manual describes as being capable of withstanding pressure equivalent to a depth of 50 meters and includes a Swim activity. In contrast, Qalo's product page says the SL-1 is water-resistant to 10 meters and warns against scuba diving and deep-water pressure. Its support site gives it a IP68 rating. In terms of temperature, the Cirqa's stated operating range is -4 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, while Qalo lists 14 to 113 degrees Fahrenheit. Qalo advertises 12 or more days of battery life for the SL-1 and Garmin up to 10 for the Cirqa. In our SL-1 review, the battery still had over half its juice left after a whole week. The Cirqa, meanwhile, charges in up to 90 minutes over a proprietary Garmin cable, while the SL-1 uses a magnetic dock with a USB-C cable. Interestingly, Qalo's docs disagree on how long it takes the SL-1 to charge: the product page says 60 to 120 minutes while the support site says two to three hours. Both bands come with an optical heart rate sensor and can measure blood oxygen, skin temperature, heart rate variability, stress and sleep stages, and both offer menstrual cycle tracking. Neither has built-in GPS, but the Cirqa can use a paired phone's GPS. Qalo rolls sleep, HRV, movement and stress into a daily "Q Score" from 1 to 100 while Garmin spreads its analyses across Body Battery, Training Readiness, training status, VO2 max and HRV status. The Cirqa lists more than 80 activity types against the SL-1's 54, and the Cirqa can broadcast heart rate to other devices. The SL-1 shares one profile with Qalo's smart rings, which the company also sells without a subscription. Qalo's product page says the SL-1's 54 activity modes include automatic activity detection, but our review found that the band didn't pick up workouts by itself, not even walks. Meanwhile, the Cirqa's automatic detection worked well enough in our testing that manual recording was rarely needed. Qalo also says its movement tracking is up to 12.5 percent more accurate than "popular alternatives." While our SL-1 review didn't test accuracy, our Cirqa review did count Garmin's reliable accuracy among the band's strengths. Beyond the specs, we found the Cirqa to be perfectly functional in our testing. That said, the single button was the main irritation, since dismissing the alarm with a mistimed press starts a workout instead. We also found the Garmin Connect app to be pretty heavy on data and light on interpretation, and it was hard to see why the Cirqa costs more than Garmin's own cheaper trackers. The SL-1 fared a little worse. The battery was excellent, still showing 59 percent after a full week, and there's no fee to worry about, but the magnetic clasp on the silicone strap can come loose if a sleeve catches it at the wrong angle, and the app does little beyond aggregating the data it collects. With both bands at the same price, we'd lean towards the Cirqa, which gets the basics right. The SL-1 would make more sense as a first screenless tracker if it were cheaper.

item.title: REVIEW: EarFun Wave Pro X Review: Budget Headphones That Punch Way Above Their Weight
item.description:
Source: PCMag
EarFun is shooting for something a little more premium with its new Wave Pro X ($129) headphones. They still fall on the more affordable side of the headphone market, but with a nicer fit and finish than you might expect. They also include premium features such as active noise cancellation, high-end codecs, and coaxial drivers. This all makes for a great set of cans, with detailed, customizable sound, useful ambient noise controls, and solid connectivity in a comfortable piece of hardware. The Wave Pro X aren’t alone, though, and you can get a lot of the same capabilities at a lower price from the $99 CMF Headphone Pro, our Editor’s Choice for budget wireless headphones. The Anker Soundcore Space Pro 2 is also a near-equal, although the Wave Pro X stands out here for its welcome granular EQ settings. The Wave Pro X headphones don’t have a terribly distinctive style. They veer away from the prior Wave Life and Wave Pro to offer something of a more elegant look, though. The metallic accents EarFun loves to include are here in the form of textured discs on the exterior of each ear cup. The headband is now almost fully cushioned and has a fabric top, likely to hide the flexible, sturdy plastic inside. The yokes are smartly designed, connecting to the earcups near the cushions for a streamlined look while wearing the headphones, and they offer plenty of swivel, rotation, and length adjustments. The earcups even fold up for storage despite the included carrying case wanting them to sit flat inside. The included case is a hardshell style with a zipper that goes around the edges. That zipper could be smoother, but otherwise it feels like a quality case to protect the headphones on the move. You might want to use the case, too, as the headphones lack official water protection (though they survived while on top of my head during a quick walk across the street in a drizzle). All this comes together to make the Wave Pro X feel like a fairly high-quality headset. Its cushioning and leatherette materials feel luxuriously soft. The instant I put the Wave Pro X on, its comfort was apparent. The gentle clamping force and plush ear cushions combined to create an almost not-there feeling, and the wide headband cushion and light 9.1-ounce weight made it feel like very little was actually resting on my head. After wearing them for about five hours straight, I still found them almost perfectly comfortable. The Wave Pro X pack in plenty, too. They include an eight-mic setup with a combination of external mics and earcup mics to handle calls, ANC, and ambient pass-through modes. Inside, EarFun has squeezed coaxial drivers, combining a 40mm driver with a 10mm one in each earcup. EarFun has three small controls on the right earcup: power, ANC, and a volume rocker. The controls feel a little cheap, but they’re fairly easy to feel and use. The power button handles power and doubles as a play/pause button, but it’s not customizable. The volume buttons can be customized, offering single-tap and long-press options. Those options are limited to just volume adjustments and skipping forward/backward in audio, though. The noise-cancelling button can cycle between settings with single taps and enable/disable Multipoint with a long press. It also supports double-tap controls but has nothing assigned by default. The Wave Pro X connects via Bluetooth 6.0 with Google Fast Pair for quick setup on Android, and it supports a wide array of codecs. You’ll get SBC and AAC for wide compatibility, but the headphones further offer LE Audio, LDAC, aptX, aptX Adaptive, and aptX Adaptive Lossless Mode. Not all of these are available at once, though. Enabling LE Audio disables LDAC, but provides Auracast support. LDAC and aptX can be enabled simultaneously. Bluetooth Multipoint is also supported, but not simultaneously with LDAC—a common and unnecessary limitation on EarFun products. That Multipoint support worked seamlessly in my testing, too, letting me switch back and forth between audio on my phone and computer with almost no delay. As I’ve found with some other EarFun models, LE Audio doesn’t appear to work at its full potential. I couldn’t get it to continue playing audio at decent quality when I engaged the microphones. I tested it on two different LE Audio-enabled laptops, and the moment the Wave Pro X's mics activated on each one, the incoming sound quality tanked—something LE Audio should have prevented. Beyond wireless connections, the headphones further support analog input with a 3.5mm jack and up to 96kHz/24-bit digital audio over USB. EarFun even includes an analog cable, though the included USB A-to-C cable is for charging only. EarFun rates the Wave Pro X headphones at 90 hours of battery life without ANC enabled, placing it between the CMF Headphone Pro (100 hours) and the Soundcore Space Pro 2 (70 hours). With ANC on, that number drops to 50 hours, which matches its competitors. If the battery drains fully, it can recharge in 2 hours with standard 5V1A charging, and the first 15 minutes of that charging are good for 10 hours of playback. It’s not specified, but these types of estimates often assume a 50% listening volume. After four hours of continuous use, I found the battery had fallen by just 5% on the Wave Pro X, putting it on track for roughly 80 hours. This may provide a little better insight into the headphones' battery life when listening at reasonable volumes. Trying to listen to speech on an airplane might require turning up the volume and relying on heavy ANC, but in quieter settings, I found that just about 25% volume was more than sufficient. The Wave Pro X works with EarFun’s app. The app doesn’t require an account to use the vast majority of its features, but if you want to use the AI Translation tool, you will need an account. I’ve found this an effective feature when testing other EarFun products, but I don’t find it a compelling selling point, given that plenty of standalone apps offer much the same capabilities, including Google Translate. Inside the app, you'll find the battery level, the ability to rename the headphones, and a ton of other settings. Up front, you'll find the ambient sound controls, which offer a normal mode (ANC off), an ambient sound mode, and the noise-cancelling mode. The ambient sound mode has three different settings, while ANC has a manual slider, two adaptive ANC modes, and a wind noise-cancelling mode. Further in, you'll find a toggle for a low-latency game mode. The app includes a pile of EQ presets as well as the option to create a custom equalizer with a basic 10-band equalizer or an advanced 10-band EQ that lets you select each frequency you want to modify (in 0.5Hz increments), the gain level (in 0.1dB increments), and the Q value (in 0.01 increments). There’s also the option to take a hearing test and create a unique sound profile. Another feature, called Sound Sense, just plays your audio and brings up the basic 10-band EQ to make a new custom setting. The app lets you customize controls, limit the max playback volume, shift the left-right balance, and decide whether you want the headphones to draw power over USB, which you might not want while they’re plugged into your phone. You'll also find settings pages for Bluetooth Multipoint, Bluetooth audio codecs, and LE Audio. The default is to enable LDAC and aptX codecs but leave Multipoint off. The app has additional settings for calls, letting you set a control to mute your mic, enable a tone to indicate when it's muted, and choose whether ambient sound plays during a call. The Wave Pro X offers a fair bit of passive isolation. They don’t mute the world entirely, or even come close, but they take the edge off some of the shrill noises around me and just lower the overall volume I’m facing, and that gives them a good starting point for noise cancellation to kick in. The ANC can then further take off a ton of the lower frequencies. In a busy cafe with a constant low-pitch hum and lots of whirring, almost all of that was canceled out. I could still hear the music playing in the cafe, some hushed mechanical noise from fridges and bean grinders, and people’s voices came through, but my surroundings were largely mellowed by the noise cancellation. Once I had music playing at a low level, I could hear very little of my surroundings. The promise that they’ll “mute the espresso machine” may not be met, but they do a darn good job otherwise. They can't do everything, though. A low 45Hz tone was hushed but audible through the headphones, whereas it almost vanished entirely in the (much more expensive) Sonos Ace. They also introduce some minor hiss at all but the lowest manual setting. Though EarFun offers adaptive ANC modes, I couldn’t quite get a read on their behavior. I toggled several test tones to see if the headphones would adapt, and almost never noticed a shift. Both adaptive modes continued to let more of a 400Hz tone through than when I manually set a lower ANC level. While it’s ultimately good noise cancellation, I wouldn’t count on it to deaden an airplane. I wouldn’t advise using ANC while you’re walking around outdoors, but if you do (or are just sitting outdoors), you’ll find the wind clipping the mics in most settings, even in light wind. For this, EarFun includes a wind noise-cancelling mode that does the trick quite well. It doesn’t hush everything quite as much, but it still reduces low, droning sounds while effectively keeping wind noise out. The behavior of the ANC isn't always perfect, though. If I make a loud snapping noise, or if two hard surfaces hit each other, the sound will blast into the headphones, and unfortunately quite loudly. I noticed this when snapping an earbud case shut, and I noticed it even more while putting silverware away. The effect is bad while ANC is active and is horrible while pass-through is active. That said, this is not unique to the Wave Pro X. I noticed the same thing from the Sonos Ace, for example. The ambient mode is nicely transparent. Its default setting boosts higher frequencies a bit too much, making for a slight hiss even in a quiet space. It also has a Natural setting that reduces the hiss. Neither is quite perfect, though, as the rattle of the headphones while I walk around produces a thumping in my ears. The Wave Pro X plays compelling bass. When The Knife’s “Silent Shout” kicks off with its bass triplets, they're tight and clean, and when the sub-bass quarter notes kick in, they're deep, full, and not overemphasized. The vocal harmonies are nice and clear, shifting back and forth with both voices presented decently well. Some of the atmospherics and pads, as well as the cymbals, get a rich presentation with plenty of air and space in the soundstage. None of the subtleties are immediately drowned out either. The high-end is modestly crisp, though still a ways off from planar magnetics, so there’s still room for improvement even with that extra 10mm driver focusing on treble. The Bruno Mars sample at the beginning of Kendrick Lamar’s “Loyalty” is fairly crisp. The drums hit hard at the start, with decent crispness on the cymbals and a good punch from the kick drum. The track introduces a deep sub-bass line at the 35-second mark, and the headphones hit all of the notes quite well. They don’t overdo it, keeping each note relatively level and even reaching down to hit the bottom note, which some headphones can still struggle with. Lamar’s and Rihanna's vocals come through perfectly clear. The headphones present the track well overall. The 10mm driver stacked onto the 40mm driver ought to help with high-end detail, as should LDAC and AptX support, but the Wave Pro X just don’t quite deliver unstoppable brilliance. Bill Callahan’s “Drover” showcases this clearly. The electric guitar, fiddle, and rhythm guitar can go from subtle texture to rich elements of the track depending on the brilliance they get. The EarFun Wave Pro X do justice to Callahan’s baritone vocals, capturing the rasp and depth. But when it comes to those accompanying instruments, they just fall a bit short of perfection. Still, it’s not bad for a $129 pair of headphones by any means. The ample range and fairly flat EQ of the Wave Pro X help it hold up well with orchestral music like John Adams’ The Gospel According to the Other Mary. Though the headphones could have better high-end performance, they provide enough detail to help the strings and brass stand out from each other. The fairly wide soundstage gives different instruments space while letting the vocals stand out, and the bass depth ensures even the deepest instruments can come through. Although the overall quality of the outgoing audio on the Wave Pro X is great for the price, the incoming audio from the mics is only average. They capture my voice clearly, but not with the crispness or richness I’d want for extended calls. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The EarFun Wave Pro X are an excellent option for the money. They have good all-around sound, capable ANC, are very comfortable, offer long battery life, and provide many ways to tune them to your liking. That may not be quite enough to set them apart from our favorite budget wireless headphones, the Editors' Choice CMF Headphone Pro, which bring similar capabilities to the mix at a slightly lower price. They also butt heads with the Anker Soundcore Space 2, which offers similar strengths and weaknesses. If you love to tune your EQ and settings, the Wave Pro X has that advantage compared with the more basic EQ found on the Anker and CMF headphones. Hopefully, EarFun can sort out its LE Audio issues to make that more of a benefit as well, since neither the CMF nor the Anker headphones offer LE Audio. Regardless, the Wave Pro X headphones are an inexpensive and compelling option. I've covered the technology field for a decade, beginning a freelance career in 2017 and working with numerous publications, including PCMag since 2021. I have reviewed hundreds of products with a particular emphasis on computers and the broad field of peripherals, especially audio gear. At PCMag, I contribute audio device reviews of products like headphones and speakers, in addition to reviews of Windows laptops.

item.title: SALES: 50 Travel Gifts Under $50 They'll Actually Use on Their Next Trip
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Travel buffs can be surprisingly difficult to shop for. They probably already have a suitcase they love, noise-canceling headphones, and enough packing cubes to last them a lifetime. Instead of adding to their collection of travel essentials, consider something they wouldn't necessarily buy for themselves. It doesn't have to be expensive, either. The best travel gifts will upgrade every journey, whether it’s a smart gadget to help make a red-eye flight less miserable or a sweet reminder of their favorite destination—all without breaking the bank. With this in mind, I’ve rounded up 50 thoughtful gifts under $50 to give this season, from personalized accessories to luxe skincare sets. Whether you're shopping for a frequent flier, an avid road tripper, or a friend with a growing list of places to visit, there's something here for every traveler on your list—including yourself. Top gifts: Every traveler needs a sturdy duffel bag for weekend road trips. This under-$30 weekender has enough space for two to three days' worth of clothes, as well as a separate shoe compartment and pockets for small travel accessories. Plus, it fits underneath a plane seat and features a luggage sleeve. This large makeup bag has earned over 13,000 reviews for its practical design, which opens flat so you can see everything inside without rummaging through it. It also has a few interior pockets, a separate brush compartment, and a water-resistant exterior that’s easy to wipe clean. L.L.Bean's classic Boat and Tote bag holds everything you need for a day trip and packs completely flat in your carry-on. It's great for storing souvenirs or to have just in case. True to its name, this bag can be used for a variety of things; it’s roomy enough to fill up with snacks, charging cords, or the jumble of in-flight necessities that usually float around in the bottom of your tote. It has a water-resistant lining and multiple interior and exterior pockets for easy access. Bagsmart's lightweight backpack is a practical gift for travelers who are always headed on a weekend getaway or could use a new personal item for the plane. Unlike a traditional backpack, it features a clamshell opening, so you can see all of your belongings at once and pack items like you would in a suitcase. The adjustable straps can even be clasped over your chest, making it more secure and comfortable. Ditch the bulky purse with this crossbody phone case, made from genuine Italian leather. It features an adjustable, removable strap you can wear crossbody or around your neck. The protective case helps guard against drops, and there's even a handy card slot on the back for your credit card or ID. It's available for iPhone 16 and 17 models. Made from 100% mulberry silk, this sleep mask feels soft against your skin while blocking out light for some much-needed shut-eye. The contoured eye cups leave room to blink without pressing on your lashes, and the adjustable strap keeps it comfortably in place. The hard outer shell of this case protects jewelry during travels, while little nooks, slot rolls, and hooks keep earrings, necklaces, and bracelets separated and tangle-free. It's small enough to pack on quick trips while being roomy enough for destination weddings and longer vacations. A weighted eye mask is a thoughtful gift for any frequent flier. This soothing mask is ideal for side sleepers or back sleepers, and keeps you comfortable at home and on the road. A reliable travel pillow is an essential on every long-haul flight. What really sets this Cabeau pillow apart from the rest is the Velcro straps on the back, designed to loop around a plane seat's headrest, helping to keep your head upright and take any pressure off your neck. This small but mighty stocking stuffer is bound to get used right away, especially if your giftee is frequently on the go. Attach it to everything from keys to luggage to keep tabs on the item using the accompanying app on your iPhone. Leakproof, magnetic, and practically indestructible, these TSA-friendly mini jars are great for decanting your toiletries, medication, or anything else that fits, for carry-on travel. Keep charging cables, earbuds, adapters, and other small tech essentials from getting lost in your bag with this leather organizer from Mark & Graham. Its slim design and snap closure make it easy to pack for trips or daily commutes. Choose from a variety of fonts, colors, and designs to customize this passport cover for the international traveler in your life. Pro tip: A bonus of going with a brighter color is that it’s easier to find in your bag when you need it. This leather luggage tag from Tumi adds a little personality to your suitcase while making it easier to spot on the baggage carousel. Available in more than 20 colors and customizable with a monogram, it's a small but thoughtful gift for frequent travelers. Available in six vibrant color combos, these handcrafted leather card cases hold up to five cards or, thanks to the snap closure, can be used to stash foreign coins that accumulate when traveling internationally. If your friend is always reading a book on their Kindle, gift them a fun case that will protect their device from accidental drops. Casely’s Kindle cover is durable yet lightweight, so they can slip it into a weekender bag or backpack without it weighing them down. This tiny, portable reading light packs a powerful punch. It attaches securely to your book and has a swiveling head with two brightness levels. Plus, it’s rechargeable via USB, with a battery life long enough to cover multiple page-turners’ worth of reading. Small enough to fit in the palm of your hand or clip onto a bag, this mini keychain camera is a fun way to capture travel memories with a nostalgic twist. It takes photos and videos, has retro-inspired filters, and comes in one of seven surprise designs. Note that you'll need to buy a memory card separately. Waterproof, dustproof, and practically everything-proof, this pocket-sized speaker is perfect for streaming your favorite tunes or podcasts while on the go. It’s available in eight fun color combos, and the best part is its durability: You can bring it on your beach vacation without worrying when it inevitably gets sandy. Owala is known for its fun-colored water bottles, but its travel mugs are equally amazing. This 12-ounce mug keeps coffee or tea hot for hours and is completely leakproof. Plus, it's available in a slew of bright colors. Whether serving your beverage neat or on the rocks, these insulated stainless steel tumblers are designed to last through countless happy hours in the backyard or backcountry. They also pack up neatly in a wool felt case for easy carrying. Lounge comfortably in your own backyard with this outdoor camping hammock. It folds down into a small storage pouch, and is incredibly lightweight while still able to hold up to 400 pounds. For any outdoorsy traveler on your list, you can't go wrong with a classic Swiss Army knife. It fits in a small fanny pack or sling bag and comes in handy for hiking or camping adventures. Rechargeable hand warmers (pack of two) A set of rechargeable hand warmers like this two-pack can keep your fingers warm for up to 12 hours on a three-hour charge, and means you don't have to abandon exploring some magnificent winter wonderland vistas due to the chill. Compact, durable, and endlessly reliable, this straw filter is an adventurer's essential—capable of transforming even the murkiest stream into safe, drinkable water. It’s the kind of smart, ultralight gear you’ll be glad to have on hand, whether you’re trekking through the backcountry or navigating an off-the-grid escape. Made from certified post-consumer recycled plastic, this ultra-absorbent towel can be used for yoga, camping, the pool, and pretty much everything in between. It’s also guaranteed to stand out on the beach courtesy of the vibrant print options available, from classic stripes to national park–inspired patterns. No need to settle for bad hotel coffee. These compact, individually packaged syrups (about the size of a tea bag) are easy to travel with, so you can perfect your morning latte every time. The variety pack includes flavors like rose vanilla, lavender honey, pistachio coconut, and salted pecan praline. A warm cardigan is an essential for chilly fall and winter mornings. Throw on this one to run errands, venture out to a museum, grab coffee (or a cocktail), and, well, pretty much anything in between. Another one of our favorite staples from Quince is this cashmere crewneck. It's super-soft, lightweight, and works for just about any winter getaway. With over 10,000 Amazon reviews, these best-selling slippers are made for cozy days at home. They have a soft, fuzzy lining, cloud-like memory foam cushioning, and nonslip soles for the occasional trip outside. Even better, they're machine washable. This sock-meet-slipper bootie has a soft brushed lining and grippy bottoms and comes in everything from heathered neutrals to festive Fair Isle patterns. Cold hands are no match for these Quince gloves, made from 100% Mongolian cashmere. The longer cuffs provide extra coverage on chilly days, while touchscreen-friendly fingertips mean you won't have to take them off every time you reach for your phone. Whether you're having a bad hair day or are just going for that model-off-duty look, Todd Snyder's Dad cap elevates any airport uniform. It's made from the same Japanese selvedge used in the brand's best-selling Chinos. These Bombas socks add a little luxury to an everyday essential with a soft, cozy blend of merino wool and cashmere. They're thick and warm without sacrificing breathability, with built-in arch support and a seamless toe for added comfort. They come in three sizes—small, medium, and large—for a more personalized fit. Socks might not seem like the most exciting gift to open on Christmas morning, but Todd Snyder's Argyle dress socks will have you thinking differently. Made in Italy with a cotton blend, they're soft and sophisticated enough for the most special of occasions. Land at your destination feeling refreshed by popping on Rhode's depuffing eye patches. These hydrating patches actually stay in place without sliding around. Give dry, tired skin a little TLC with the Summer Fridays Jet Lag Essentials Set, featuring four travel-size bestsellers: a hydrating face mist, serum, moisturizing mask, and depuffing eye patches. This limited-edition Rhode set pairs the brand's creamy Pocket Blush with its glossy Peptide Lip Tint for an easy pop of color on the go. Both formulas are hydrating and buildable, and the set comes in three coordinated shade combinations, from soft pink to warm brown to mauve. Keep dry hands soft and moisturized on the go with this L'Occitane gift set. It includes three travel-sized hand creams made in France, featuring the brand's signature shea butter, warm almond, and calming lavender scents. They're just the right size to tuck into a purse, carry-on, or desk drawer. Whether you’re looking for relief after a marathon of luggage-laden travel or a little help unwinding from back-to-back Zoom meetings, this soothing botanical blend of lavender, ginger root, and geranium provides just the right dose of self-care in a TSA-approved rollerball size. Pro tip: Dab it on your pulse points and pair with an eye mask and noise-canceling headphones for brief moments of zen. There’s nothing more relaxing than a soothing scalp massage. This beautiful, weighty comb is carved from jade (and comes in varying shades of serene green). It is designed to relieve tension and help stimulate circulation. It’s perfect for pairing with your favorite hair treatment for a calming self-care ritual. Infused with aloe and botanical extracts, this skin-softening cleanser from New York City–based Le Labo can be used head-to-toe—taking a simple act of hygiene to the next level with its classic yet luxurious scent of lavender, bergamot, and violet. Formulated with five ultra-nourishing oils and butters (cocoa, sweet almond, apricot kernel, fractionated coconut, and avocado), this sculptural moisturizer softens as it comes into contact with warm, dry skin. Bask in the calming mix of woody vetiver and zesty bergamot, and use it as a massage stone for an incredibly relaxing and indulgent self-care ritual that rivals a day at your favorite spa. Give the gift of great skin with Merit Beauty's best-selling serum. This mini size is TSA-approved and fits nicely in any Dopp kit. Merit's Flush cream blush is just the right size to keep in your purse for quick, on-the-go touches. It melts effortlessly into the skin and makes blending in your blush easier than ever. Raw, sustainably sourced, and utterly therapeutic, these wildcrafted honeys are hand-harvested from apiaries around the country. Break up the set to gift as foodie stocking stuffers—or hoard one or two for yourself. These beautiful color-blocked teaspoons from Australian brand Fazeek are hand-blown from durable borosilicate glass, and are useful for drizzling toppings or mixing concoctions. They make for a memorable gift for the foodie friend who has everything. Bring a taste of the Italian coast home with this Voluspa candle, which blends bright scents of Sicilian lemon and bergamot with notes of jasmine and warm amber. item.title: REVIEW: Anker Eufy Window Camera E10 Review: A Weirdly Good ‘Outdoor’ Camera
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
If you’re lucky and privileged enough to own a home, your options for outdoor security cameras are many. But not everyone is in that position, and although you can get away with using many smart home gadgets in a rental, security cameras will be a no-go for most people, especially apartment dwellers. The Eufy Window Camera E10 is aimed at those people, or more accurately, the people walking past their homes. For an $80 camera, the E10 is very nice. It offers 2.5K video, onboard local storage via microSD, and fast, dual-band Wi-Fi. Best of all, you don’t need a single tool to install it; it just sticks to the inside of your window. I have some concerns about the idea of pointing any such device outward from an apartment building, but if you live in a rental house and have permission from your landlord—or heck, if you own your home but just don’t feel like drilling holes in your exterior fascia—and you’re willing to understand and accept some limitations, it’s a pretty neat product. I got an early look at an E10, and despite some obvious shortcomings, it’s one of my favorite security cameras that I’ve tested in years. A surprisingly capable, easy-to-install wired camera that works well in the right context. - Reflections can be a problem on dual-pane windows Who needs a drill? The best thing about the Window Camera E10 is how easy it is to install. All you have to do is clean the dust and dirt off your window, place its mounting sticker on there, and then slap the camera onto its hook-and-loop side. There’s even a second sticker in case you don’t like where you put the camera the first time and want to move it. I installed it in a kitchen window that overlooks my backyard and is close to a countertop outlet in an out-of-the-way corner. This camera’s small, but still an eyesore, especially with a cable dangling from it, although Anker does at least include stick-on cable clips to deal with that. I was done with the window-cleaning and camera-sticking parts of this process in just a couple of minutes. Adding the camera to the Anker Eufy app was fast, too—I searched for it in the app, tapped it when it appeared, and went through the Wi-Fi setup. If you have a compatible Eufy HomeBase device, you can connect the camera to that instead. With or without support, I wouldn’t buy a HomeBase just for this camera—it adds local storage, but you can get plenty of that for less money by buying a microSD card. (The Window Camera E10 supports cards of up to 256GB.) The hub does add HomeKit Secure Video support to certain Eufy cameras, such as the EufyCam S3 Pro, but that’s not the case for the Window Camera E10—you only get Alexa and Google Assistant support here, with or without a Eufy hub. You can get facial recognition if you have a HomeBase S380, but that costs $200. Once you’re set up, you can manually adjust the Window Camera E10’s vertical angle by up to 25 degrees using a small mechanical dial on the back. The camera has a 125-degree field of view—which is good, not great, but was plenty in my testing position, which was mounted about 10 feet off the ground. Anker’s app isn’t stuffed with features, but it hits the right notes. You can adjust the camera’s video streaming quality, create blacked-out privacy zones by drawing shapes on the feed, and adjust motion-detection sensitivity. It includes individual toggles that enable push notifications when the camera detects people, vehicles, pets, or general motion, as well as separate buttons that control whether each event category is recorded. The camera has a rolling buffer and supports prerecording, in which it appends footage of the few seconds prior to videos of events that it detects. That consistently prevented the device from producing recordings that captured only half of what had happened, an issue that has plagued many older smart home cameras I’ve tested, including Anker’s own EufyCam 2C Pro. You can also configure the app to send push notifications that contain text alone, for speed, or thumbnails with text if you don’t mind waiting a bit. A balanced mode sends text notifications separately from thumbnails, and that’s the one I’d use. The text-based messages arrive quickly—within about four seconds, which is as fast as I’ve seen with any smart home security camera—and indicate whether the camera has detected a person, vehicle, animal, or generic motion, depending on which is toggled on. That detection happens on-device. There are also a couple of surprising features for a camera at this price point, like the ability to record 24/7, though the app could make clearer how to view this ongoing footage. To do so, you have to either tap a small icon in the Anker Eufy Security tab or open the camera you want to look at, tap its name, and then tap “Playback.” That seems like a button that should just be available at the bottom of the camera view, next to the buttons for recording, taking screenshots, changing the resolution, and starting a timelapse. If you don’t want to deal with local storage, Anker offers plans that start at $3.33 per month for 30 days of video history on a single camera and up to 180 days and unlimited cameras for $41.66 per month. Weird pricing, but it’s not bad when compared to the options from companies like Arlo and Ring. I prefer to stick with local recording, given smart home cameras’ repeated software security problems, Anker’s among them. If you’re curious to read more about that, there’s a good summary over at The Verge, which reported in 2022 and 2023 about unencrypted camera streams on Eufy cameras. Anker, to its credit, made a number of changes as a result of that reporting, and now has a whole page devoted to the steps it takes to ensure its devices respect your privacy. High-quality imagery, but reflections can be a big problem The Window Camera E10’s body acts as a shroud for the camera sensor, preventing any reflections from getting between it and the pane of glass it’s stuck on. Most of the surrounding area has a matte finish, although the little half-globe part that the camera sits in is glossy, which I worried would lead to unnecessary glare. It didn’t in my case, but that doesn’t mean this wasn’t an issue—far from it. Things were fine when the sun wasn’t touching the window. The image was as clear as it would be with any outdoor-mounted security camera. But as soon as the afternoon sun touched a bright green wall perpendicular to the window, I could see a faint image of the wall in the outer edge of the E10’s video. It didn’t screw with most of the image, but I wouldn’t put this device on a window that gets direct sun for long stretches of the day. The reflections got much worse at night. When I turned the kitchen light on, a partial halo of light filled the bottom and side edges of the image. I could tell the shrouded design of the Window Camera E10 was doing its job because there was a hard border inside the halo where the camera’s body blocked the light, but it wasn’t enough to make the outer edge of its picture easily visible. Anker includes an extra set of opaque, matte-black stickers shaped to sit around the outside of the hook-and-loop you attach the E10 to, widening the area of light it blocks. Those help quite a bit, though they also make the thing more of an eyesore. An easier solution would be just to lower your blinds or close the curtain behind the camera. Reflections aside, the Window Camera E10 produced very clear, sharp video by day, with little of the artifacting you might see with older or cheaper smart home security cameras. The E10’s sensor is still not as sharp as what a modern smartphone can produce—they never are—but its picture is crisper than what I got from the Tapo Doorbell Pro D260 and close to as good as that of the Reolink Elite Floodlight WiFi I tried last year. At night, the image was a lot muddier. The Window Camera E10 lacks any sort of spotlight, infrared or otherwise, so it’s doing the best it can with its visible camera sensor. I wouldn’t count on it to identify intruders without a bright floodlight in the area it’s watching. I came into this review expecting that, given its price, the Window Camera E10 would be a mediocre device that’s serviceable for something like checking your porch to see if a package has arrived but little else. Instead, I came away impressed by its video quality and breadth of features. It has a stable, fast Wi-Fi connection, and I appreciate its multiple local storage options and quick detection of people, animals, and vehicles. Left: Night shot without light-blocking stickers. Right: With the stickers, reflections are so much better. © Wes Davis / Gizmodo I wish the Window Camera E10 also had package detection, and it’s a shame that it isn’t compatible with Apple Home, even when connected to one of Anker’s Eufy HomeBase hubs. Its night vision is blurry and not particularly useful without other bright exterior lights, and reflections can be a big problem in a house with dual-pane windows. It’s also silly that it has a speaker and microphone at all—I’m sure you could hear a person talking through an old, single-pane window, but I doubt they’d hear you very well unless the window is actually open. Lastly, the fact that it’s wired is inconvenient because it limits you to placing the camera somewhere where its 10-foot USB-C-to-USB-A cable can reach an outlet. Still, I expected all of those shortcomings and was surprised I didn’t run into more. This is a capable little $80 wired camera, and one I’d recommend to anyone who just wants an easy way to check their front porch for packages when they’re away from home or peek at their backyard to make sure they remembered to close their fence. It’s not exactly a security camera, but not everything has to be.

item.title: REVIEW: If Snap’s Specs are still ridiculously expensive, they’re also a lot more comfortable than they used to be
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
When I tried a prototype of Snap’s Specs at CES in Las Vegas earlier this year, the experience left something to be desired. The company’s AR glasses — which the company calls a “new kind of computer” — were heavy (they weighed around 8 ounces) and fit rather uncomfortably on my face. The device was also hot, and made my face feel tingly — a common side-effect of smart glasses where massive computing is happening under the hood. Fast forward to late October, when I met back up with the Snap team at a Four Seasons in downtown San Francisco. By this time, the company had debuted Specs publicly during an event with CEO Evan Spiegel, and pre-orders of the company’s long-gestating headset were already underway. What I can say is this: Specs has improved the form factor significantly since my first brush with the device. The glasses now weigh nearly half of what the previous version did, slimming down to 132 grams, or approximately 4.6 ounces. They were quite comfortable and, during the hour-ish that I demo-ed the device, it did not heat up like the previous version had. Specs now comes in two sizes — 47mm and 52mm. The purpose here is purely to accommodate different head sizes, ensuring the glasses fit snugly on whoever’s face happens to be wearing them. They also now come equipped with spring hinges, which make the device more flexible and comfortable. However, if the body of the device has improved greatly, its soul is still a work-in-progress. The glasses can be fun — but they also still seem to lack a dedicated purpose, and one struggles to imagine how, specifically, this expensive head gear ($2,200 a pop) would prove useful in a daily capacity. When I asked Snap staff what the device was really for — fun and games or productivity — the answer was vague. The device attempts to be a bunch of things at once and, in the process, ends up feeling a little rudderless. I have racked my brain to come up with some daily use-cases for Specs. Some of the things I came up with were: - Watching TV or movies while you’re on a train or some other form of public transportation. There are places where you just have to hang out for awhile and, not infrequently, one way to pass the time is streaming. Specs provides a much more immersive form of mobile entertainment than simply watching a video on your cell phone. The device’s integrations with HBO Max and YouTube make it an appealing entertainment option for users who are in-transit. - Reading. Because of the immersive nature of Snap’s headset, I feel like they could be a good option for reading while traveling. When you’re reading with Specs, it feels like you’re locked into whatever text you happen to be looking at. It weirdly helped me focus. An integration for newspapers or Kindle could make the glasses a good way to read while you’re mobile (I’m envisioning the ideal setting being on a plane, train, or the back of a car). - Taking easily shareable weird videos. Like many of Meta’s smart glasses, Specs allows users to take photographs and videos, which is an odd but fun component of the user experience. The ability to generate GoPro-like videos and easily text them to your friends is something that I could see the casual user doing on a somewhat regular basis. By contrast, here are some of the areas I’m still not totally sold on as Specs use-cases: - Specs as a daily workspace and productivity tool. Snap is selling Specs as a way to work. The company claims its headset can “transform almost any location into an immersive, flexible workspace.” However, I have a really hard time imagining Specs being something that the average worker is going to want to incorporate into their workflows. It’s less convenient to strap the glasses to your head than it is to simply sit at your computer typing. What can Specs provide that a cell phone and laptop can’t? The social stigma of wearing weird, large glasses and gesticulating to operate them would also seem to be a deterrent. - A widely used gaming device. Due to the prohibitive cost of the device (again, nearly $2200), I have a really hard time imagining that there is going to be a huge audience for Specs as a gaming device. Most Xboxes are under half the price of this device. Are the games on Specs fun? Sure, kind of. But are teenagers going to be clamoring for them come Christmas time? That I’m not so sure about. Specs is impressive for how the Snap team has managed to integrate a variety of user experiences into one unified device. There are a lot of impressive achievements here — specifically the spatial synching tech that allows two users to see the same thing simultaneously — that, with some further development, could be deployed towards some really interesting use cases. The bottom line is that Snap’s device can continue to grow and transform as the company iterates. It’s an interesting product that — like a lot of its peers — doesn’t necessarily seem to have a clear purpose but, in time, could become many things. What the device currently offers, however, may not be compelling enough to encourage people to shell out the cash that Snap is asking for.

item.title: REVIEW: Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 review: Infinity Ward finally returns to making a good CoD game
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
“Modern Warfare 4 reminds me why I fell in love with Call of Duty, even if a few old frustrations haven't quite gone away.”
Being a Call of Duty fan in recent years has felt nothing short of being trapped in a toxic relationship. Most titles over the past few years have disappointed me, lacking creativity and authenticity. But truth be told, how creative can you honestly get with a Call of Duty title at this point? The player base is pretty much galvanized, and we have all seen that going futuristic is not the answer, so I was pretty pumped when Activision announced the reboot of the Modern Warfare games back in 2019. The first two games were genuinely among the best the franchise has managed to put out in a long while, but along came the third game and all that newfound hope went out the window. Whatever residual hopium I had in my system was drained by the blunder that was Black Ops 7. Dreading the worst, I still paid $70 for the recently released Modern Warfare 4 just out of sheer curiosity. As it turns out, my questionable financial judgment finally paid off. The campaign in this new game has been a breath of fresh air, with great visuals, a respectable storyline, and zero filler missions. Multiplayer, while not the experience that makes me sink the entire weekend glued to my PC, is still solid, especially with new modes like Collateral, Kill Block, and Inflation. The real standout for me in this game has been DMZ. Between the skill trees, bounty boards, and a solid variety of missions, it is the mode I have enjoyed the most in this new entry. Modern Warfare 4’s campaign plays out as two stories stitched together. Price seems to have followed in the footsteps of Jason Bourne and Frank Castle, going after whatever’s left of Makarov’s operation while partnering with some unsavory people. The other side involves the invasion of South Korea by the North, and you spend a good portion of the game playing as a Korean soldier who never wanted to be a conscript but is now somehow in the middle of this full-scale incursion. Archer ties into both sides of the story and plays the puppet master, pushing his ultranationalist agenda to expand Russian influence and break Western dominance. The invasion plays out in the present, while Price’s missions jump back to the days leading up to it, so you’re often piecing together how things got this bad while the war is already raging. I am not a big fan of this back-and-forth storytelling, but to the studio’s credit, they managed to do it in a way that didn’t feel forced or extremely confusing. The two sides also play very differently. Price’s missions feel personal and grimy, with a lot of hand-to-hand combat, while the Korean ones are basically all-out war with tanks, explosions, and the takeover of entire cities. When the two stories finally crash into each other near the end, it really does feel like Infinity Ward wrapping up the MW saga. We all remember the iconic moment during the mission “Going Dark” in Modern Warfare 2019 where Price tells Gaz, “You draw the line wherever you need it, Sergeant,” in the context of using extreme measures such as collateral damage to complete their mission. At the time, it played out as a hard-earned lesson from a veteran who had seen a lot and knew that sometimes hard decisions were needed to ensure success. Soap’s death has clearly broken something in him, and you see it throughout the story. Seven years later, Price seems to have wandered so far past that line that he has all but forgotten to draw it. Soap’s death has clearly broken something in him, and you see it throughout the story. It all starts to become clear pretty early on as he kills Makarov with his bare hands in an alley after chasing him through New York’s streets and rooftops. From that moment, it’s clear this isn’t the same man we’ve followed since 2019. After that, he teams up with Valeria Garza and her cartel in a bid to hunt down Archer, the Russian defense minister. The partnership takes him through messy fights across the streets of Paris and close-quarters chases through Mumbai, where the cartel’s reckless disregard for civilian casualties constantly clashes with Price’s attempts to keep people out of harm’s way. Price does his best to keep them clear of the chaos, but it feels like he is fighting a losing battle. The arguments between him and Valeria are some of the more interesting moments in this storyline. Underneath all the shouting, Price seems to be trying to convince himself that he’s still doing all this for the greater good. He has fully bought into the ends justify the means mindset. On the other side, the invasion doesn’t just come out of nowhere. It begins with a purge of traitors within the North Korean camp before turning into a power grab by Ri Ju-Young, who isn’t content being the sister of the newly appointed Supreme Leader. She sees herself as the stronger leader, someone ruthless enough to maintain an empire built on fear and authoritarian control. Her brother’s comparatively softer side only makes him look weak in her eyes. In one of the darkest scenes of the campaign, she takes control of the country and comes up with a “simple plan” to overrun their southern counterpart. Archer is at the center of this political coup. He offers Russian backing and frames the invasion as a war to reunite the Korean peninsula. He also provides North Korea with an experimental, single-use EMP designed to cripple South Korean infrastructure, electricity, and military communications. For Archer, the invasion doubles as a proving ground for a weapon he eventually wants to use against American influence across East Asia. While the core cast is as reliable as ever, what pleasantly surprised me was how well the Korean characters were written. Park Hyun Jun is serving his mandatory military service when the war lands on his doorstep. From that moment on, all he is trying to do is keep his squad alive, which makes him an easy character to root for. Ko Jin-Hyuk, a North Korean officer, has spent most of his life doing what he’s told. But after witnessing the brutality of Ri’s regime up close, he slowly starts making his own choices, and I found myself getting more invested in him with every mission. Ri Ju-Young, meanwhile, makes herself the kind of villain that’s easy to hate, which is precisely her role. In one mission, you play as a North Korean infantry soldier, and she forces you into a decision that is demonic at its core and something you don’t agree with. It’s quite an uncomfortable stretch, and it makes it very easy to understand why someone like Ko might eventually want her out. It really feels like a missed opportunity to have an actor of his caliber and give him so little to do. Mads Mikkelsen’s Archer is the complete opposite. He plays his role brilliantly and brings a cold, menacing presence to every scene he’s part of. The issue comes when there aren’t more of those scenes. He is criminally underutilized. You never feel invested in Archer the same way you do with the others, and you don’t really learn what drives him until the end. He never gets a proper chance to establish his presence in the limelight, which reminded me of Mikkelsen’s role as Kaecilius in Doctor Strange. It really feels like a missed opportunity to have an actor of his caliber and give him so little to do. There is a lot of action packed into the approximately eight-hour campaign, and I rarely felt like I was slogging through a boring mission just to get to the end. The environments across the world look strikingly similar to their real-life counterparts, and the graphics are definitely an underappreciated aspect of the game. The gunplay has a real weight to it, similar to Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2. Every shot lands with a satisfying impact, helped by the aim punch effect and screen shake. All of it adds to the immersion and makes the firefights feel considerably more intense. The boldest, and my clear favorite addition to the campaign is Stranded, a single open-world mission set behind enemy lines in snowy North Korea, where you scavenge, craft, and tackle three main objectives however you like. It honestly felt like its own game mode, so I have discussed it in detail separately. The mission right after it goes in the opposite direction, and it’s just as memorable. With evac on its way, you have to hold your ground, switching between members of the squad to deal with ambushes, tanks, and snipers picking at you from a distance. Jumping between positions to plug whatever gap opens up makes you feel like you’re running the whole defense like a strategy game rather than playing one soldier. It’s a great payoff after the slower pace of Stranded, and one of my favorite sequences in the campaign. The campaign is far from perfect, though. Price’s arc carries so much weight early on but loses focus as the Korean conflict takes over, and the ending doesn’t land with quite the emotional punch it’s reaching for. The one-on-one melee fights feel like a two-button simulator, where you block, hit back, and repeat until it’s over. The final showdown with Archer is over almost as soon as it begins, and it doesn’t come close to the iconic finale of the original Modern Warfare 3 back in 2011, where Price finally gets his hands on Makarov. PC performance was the other sore spot. I was playing on max graphics with a rig well above the recommended specs, and the game still didn’t run as smoothly as it should have. Things only settled down once I turned on DLSS and frame generation. A good campaign mode is always appreciated, but what ultimately makes or breaks a Call of Duty title is the multiplayer mode. After all, most players finish the campaign within a week at most and then go on to sink hundreds, if not thousands, of hours into matchmaking for the rest of the year. It’s also the part of the franchise that has been in desperate need of some innovation. The biggest noticeable change for me was the movement. Infinity Ward has dropped the omnimovement mechanics first introduced in Black Ops 6 for something a lot more realistic. You can no longer slide in any direction other than the one you’re facing, which gives the gameplay a more grounded feel. You’re not nearly as quick on your feet as in some of the recent titles, but slides and slide cancels still let you chain together movement that feels fast and responsive. I actually preferred this approach. The movement feels more deliberate, and positioning matters more than simply being able to throw yourself around the map. The studio has nailed the gunplay in terms of mechanics, and recoil animations actually match how the guns behave. Unfortunately, inconsistent shot registration has been a recurring source of frustration in many of my matches. Time to kill is also slower than in previous Modern Warfare titles but faster than in the Black Ops franchise, and it lands perfectly in the Goldilocks zone. You rarely feel like you got deleted without even having a chance, but you also never feel the need to empty an entire magazine into someone just to get a kill. There has been a lot of discord around matchmaking in online forums and threads, but my experience was quite different. I found matchmaking to be extremely reliable, and most of my games came down to the wire. The final scores were usually close enough that either team could have won, with the result often coming down to a few clutch moments. Anyone coming into the game expecting to farm clips by running circles around less experienced players might be in for a surprise. Matchmaking adjusts to your skill level pretty quickly, and games become considerably more competitive after that. I enjoyed the challenge, even if it meant I couldn’t always have a relaxing evening mowing down entire lobbies. The game has a total of 13 6v6 maps following the recent addition of Shipment, and most of them are solid, with a couple of glaring exceptions. Transit is far too small to be enjoyable, which is odd considering none of the other maps are particularly big to begin with. Nautical also feels like a worse version of Hijacked. A few additional flanking paths could make it more viable for competitive gameplay. The rest will take some time to learn, but I enjoyed most of them. Infinity Ward has also introduced several new multiplayer modes, and some of them are genuinely interesting. Collateral is the most tactical of the bunch, a 5v5 take on Search and Destroy without respawns or custom loadouts. Every match begins with a pistol round, and you buy extra gear using money earned through kills and bomb plants. Anyone familiar with Counter-Strike or Valorant will feel right at home. Hijack is a little simpler. Both teams fight over a single Data Spike that can be carried, thrown, or passed between players. The objective is to plant it at the enemy’s Comm Station and defend it until the upload finishes. Inflation is a fast-paced 6v6 respawn mode where every kill increases your cash level. The richer you get, the bigger a target you become, and once you cross a certain threshold, your location becomes visible to everyone on the radar. All three are welcome additions, but Kill Block is where I think Infinity Ward has gotten a little more creative. It’s a modular, three-section mode set in a training facility. The outer sections are pulled from a broad pool of custom-built environments, while the central section often features iconic locations from classic Call of Duty maps such as Crash, Shoot House, Highrise, and Kill House. The modular design allows for more than 500 combinations, which does a surprisingly good job of keeping matches fresh. Some sections even bring their own snow or rain, reducing visibility and making long sightlines a lot less reliable. You can’t always rely on knowing the map inside out, and I enjoyed having to adapt my approach from one match to the next. Weapon progression has also received some much-needed attention. MW4 introduces cross-weapon attachment progression, which means you can gain weapon levels on guns you don’t use if they share an attachment with one you do. It cuts down on a lot of repetitive grinding and makes experimenting with different weapons considerably more rewarding. Maxing out a gun also unlocks its Apex attachment, which can completely change how the weapon plays without taking up one of the five attachment slots. Custom loadouts still offer three built-in perks and a huge variety of killstreak rewards, ranging from the familiar UAV to a railgun sentry and a gunship. There is plenty to experiment with, although the fundamentals will feel familiar to anyone who has spent time with the series. I’ve already sunk around 40 hours into multiplayer, and unfortunately, it’s starting to feel a little repetitive. Kill Block keeps things fresh, and the new modes have their moments, but I don’t find myself itching to jump back in the way I did with some of the older Modern Warfare games. The gunplay is excellent, movement feels good, and matchmaking has been reliable, but the novelty of the new modes can only carry the experience so far. If Infinity Ward wants me to put in hundreds of hours as I did with its earlier titles, it will need to keep the new ideas coming throughout the year, not just at launch. Out of all the modes available, DMZ is the one that kept me hooked the longest. The map is bigger than ever before, with more progression options, a social hub, and interesting missions. It is set after the events of the campaign and drops up to 60 players in squads of three into an open-world sandbox where you fight other operators as well as AI forces standing in your way. That sandbox is Hajin, a demilitarized zone between North and South Korea. It is the largest DMZ map yet, with 13 major points of interest and 60 smaller locations, each carrying different threat levels. Dynamic weather also plays a much bigger role than before, affecting visibility and sightlines during adverse conditions. Vehicles now need refueling and repairs, which makes gas stations important pit stops and, naturally, prime camping grounds for tryhards. There are only six story missions at launch, which leaves a lot to be desired in terms of quantity, but the missions themselves offer plenty of variety. Operation Silent Ledger involves a heist at the Heavenly Luck Casino in search of master printing plates secured inside its vault. Operation Fallen Ember has you infiltrating the heavily irradiated Haneul Nuclear Reactor to release its lockdown. It involves pulling out spent fuel rods and securing a nuclear warhead before making your escape across the water. Each mission pays out 25,000 cash plus keys, gear, and even vehicles. On top of that, Dynamic Ops are multi-stage missions you can pick up mid-match or select at your FOB before deploying. Rewards improve with every stage, and finishing the final one calls in a high-tier supply drop. Killing other players raises your heat level, which works similarly to the wanted system in Grand Theft Auto. The higher your heat, the bigger the bounty on your head. Anyone willing to pay for the information can track you through bounty boards scattered across the map. You can also visit one yourself to pay off your own bounty or buy intel on other targets. It adds another layer of risk to engaging other players, since winning a fight can end up making the rest of your deployment considerably more dangerous. Between deployments, you head back to your FOB, a safe haven where you prepare for the next run. New stations unlock as you level up, including vendors, a 3D printer, and a dog tag case. There is also a firing range to test your weapons. In a squad, everyone joins the leader’s FOB. You can no longer buy gear mid-match, so anything you want to craft has to be scavenged first. It puts a lot more weight on looting and exploring, and I found myself paying considerably more attention to what I picked up during each deployment. DMZ progression is also kept completely separate from multiplayer. After reaching level 10, you unlock the Gunsmith station, which allows you to craft more customization options and weapons based on manuals gathered during your operations in Hajin. Every additional attachment slot has to be purchased, and each one costs more than the last. The stakes get considerably higher as you invest more into your weapon. A fully kitted gun will win you more head-to-head fights, but you also run the risk of getting blindsided early and losing everything you’ve invested in it. Operators work the same way. Each has three trait trees, Warfighter, Scout, and Survivalist, that grow the longer you survive. Die, and that operator is lost unless you pay for a rescue team, which gets more expensive the higher their level. I love how much weight this gives to every decision. You can spend hours building up an operator and putting together the perfect loadout, only for one badly judged fight to undo all that work. It can be frustrating, but the possibility of losing everything is also what makes a successful extraction so satisfying. My biggest complaint is that DMZ doesn’t really cater to solo players. You can turn off squad fill and go in alone, but you could still run into a three-stack of sweats coordinating over Discord. Leaving squad fill enabled pairs you with random players, but that rarely matches the coordination of a group that plays together every night. I don’t mind the challenge of going in alone, but a dedicated solo queue would make the mode considerably more approachable without taking away the tension. DMZ is also no longer free to play. It’s part of the $70 game, and given how much work has gone into it, I think that’s fair. What bothers me is that the $100 Vault Edition includes single-use DMZ upgrades. They’re minor right now, but it feels like a slippery slope toward pay-to-win and sends the wrong message to players who have already paid full price. Still, you can get a ton of value out of DMZ. The progression is incredibly rewarding, and there’s always the thrill of knowing one bad decision could cost you a lot of it. It’s the closest Call of Duty has come to RPG-style immersion, and I absolutely love it. I wouldn’t be surprised if DMZ ends up being the main reason many people buy the game, because it’s certainly the biggest reason I keep coming back. If this is indeed the last title in the rebooted Modern Warfare saga, it’s a great send-off by Infinity Ward. The campaign outshines its predecessor by a mile and feels like a return to the series’ roots, full of enthralling action and moments that remind you why this franchise defined a generation of shooter games. It does miss the mark in a few places. Archer deserved considerably more screen time, Price’s character arc loses some of its momentum, and the final encounter is underwhelming. Even so, the stakes feel real, the two storylines come together convincingly, and I enjoyed almost every hour of it. Multiplayer nails the fundamentals. Movement is grounded, guns feel responsive, and new modes like Kill Block, Collateral, and Inflation offer a welcome change of pace. The foundation is solid, but Infinity Ward will need to keep introducing fresh ideas through seasonal updates if it wants to keep players like me invested six months from now. The real star of the show, though, is DMZ. It’s easily the mode that ate up most of my hours and the one I see myself sticking with the longest. The progression is rewarding, the environment is excellent, and the constant risk of losing everything makes even an ordinary deployment exciting. I just wish solo players had a fairer shot, and Activision would keep gameplay advantages out of its premium editions. After years of disappointing releases, I genuinely wasn’t expecting to enjoy Modern Warfare 4 this much. I still have my complaints, and I’m not entirely convinced multiplayer will keep me coming back all year, but for once, my annual $70 contribution to Activision’s bottom line feels like money well spent.
