item.title: REVIEW: Ninja’s AutoBarista is impressively versatile, but one feature was a dealbreaker for me
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
I’ve made about a dozen different kinds of coffee drinks with the Ninja AutoBarista, and I have absolutely no idea what sort of grind size, tamping pressure, water temperature, or extraction timing is necessary to pull espresso shots for any of those drinks. The AutoBarista takes care of these considerations for you, making it possible to brew 13 different drinks with just the press of a button. The AutoBarista seeks to create the experience of having a coffee shop inside of your home, but without having to master the complicated, time-consuming nuances of making perfect espresso. It makes drip coffee and espresso-and-milk drinks, like cappuccinos or flat white. The fully automatic espresso machine can even make a pretty fast cold brew or cold-pressed espresso (just add ice, or else it’s more like lukewarm brew). The AutoBarista’s versatility comes from its “Grind iQ” feature. This technology allows the machine to pick up on your coffee bean size, roast type, and freshness, auto-calibrating the grind size, weight, and dose of each brew to make your drink of choice. As you customize the number of shots in your drink, the intensity of the shot, and the temperature, Grind iQ adjusts as well. If using something like Grind iQ sounds like bowling with the bumpers up, or playing Mario Kart with steer assist, then this is not a machine for you — stick with your pour overs and enjoy your gooseneck electric kettle. This is not a machine for coffee snobs who want to control every last detail of the brewing process. Rather, it’s for people who love coffee, but have never analyzed their espresso pucks. With the caveat that I am not invested in the coffee brewing process, I will say that I think the AutoBarista makes good drinks. On one side of the machine, it can pull shots of espresso or brew drip coffee, while on the other, it has an automatic milk frother and stainless steel pitcher, which allows you to customize settings based on your desired temperature and heaviness of the foam. It also includes a setting for frothing plant-based milk. To keep the coffee tasting good, the AutoBarista always rinses itself before and after making a drink. This is a useful feature — I often find myself manually running water through my Nespresso machine, since I don’t use it every day. But the water catches in a drip tray, which fills up after making just a few drinks, so if you live with another person, then emptying the tray will be a daily nuisance. While the design of the machine makes it easy to pull out the tray, I’ve accidentally overfilled it and spilled coffee-tinted water on my kitchen floor more than once. That’s the dealbreaker. When you pull out the drip tray, you’ll also see the knock box, which collects your spent espresso pucks. Be warned: if you forget to empty the knock box for even just a few days, you may get jump-scared by some blue mold next time you go to dump the pucks. Maybe I should’ve seen that coming, but scrubbing the moldy knock box made me feel ready to go back to my beloved OXO Cold Brew Coffee Maker, which costs just six percent of the price of the AutoBarista. In the AutoBarista’s defense, most people probably wouldn’t find this machine so arduous to care for. I just happen to be someone who makes one big batch cold brew every other week and tries to keep my morning rituals minimal. If you have more patience than I do before 8 AM, then you may very well love this machine and find it low maintenance. Ninja excels at making multi-use kitchen products, and the AutoBarista is no exception, combining a drip coffee maker, espresso machine, milk frother, and grinder, and food scale into one device. But if you’re not planning to take advantage of the AutoBarista’s versatility, then it’s not worth paying its $999.99 price.

item.title: REVIEW: Seagate One Touch Portable Review: Spinning Platters to Save Some Dollars
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The Seagate One Touch Portable (starts at $159.99 for 2TB; $199.99 for 4TB, as tested) is a new external hard drive that couldn't come at a better time. Because storage price hikes due to the ongoing global memory shortage have disproportionately affected solid-state drives (SSDs), old-school spinning hard drives—although plodding—are seeing renewed interest. The One Touch Portable offers highly portable storage at less than half the price of an external SSD with equivalent capacity from a major manufacturer. It has good throughput for a small-format hard drive in two of our tests, but posted a so-so score in a third test that measures a drive's aptitude for general storage tasks. The fact that the One Touch Portable maxes out at 4TB, not 6TB, means it doesn't unseat the WD My Passport as our Editors' Choice pick for external hard drives. But it's still price relief in these fraught times for storage costs. Earlier this year, Seagate launched its first 8TB bus-powered external hard drives, the One Touch and the FireCuda X Vault. They need no power adapter, drawing juice from their host computer over the same connection used to exchange data. While those two hard drives can be easily carried in a travel bag or backpack, they use 3.5-inch drive mechanisms and weigh at least 2.5 pounds each. The smaller, lighter One Touch Portable, which presumably uses a 2.5-inch mechanism inside (Seagate doesn't specify its size), can fit in a pants pocket. It measures 0.6 by 3.2 by 4.6 inches (HWD) and weighs just under 6 ounces. These are more typical dimensions and weight for a portable hard drive. Our review unit, shown in the photos here, comes in dark blue; it is also available in gray or white. About a third of the drive—on the top, bottom, sides, and one end—is smooth; the rest is clad in a handsome wavelike texture that is easy to grip. At one end is a USB-C port, with a small status light next to it. A USB-C-to-USB-C cable, about 18 inches long, is included. The One Touch Portable comes in 2TB and 4TB capacities, at the list prices and cost per gigabyte shown below. Its cost per gigabyte is in line with other portable hard drives at those capacities. Portable hard drives—ones with 2.5-inch drive mechanisms—come in capacities up to 6TB. These include two Editors' Choice models—the WD My Passport Ultra and WD My Passport, Works with USB-C—and the SanDisk Professional G-Drive ArmorATD. We are not aware of any portable 2.5-inch HDDs with 6TB capacities from other brands. Seagate has brought some 5TB portable hard drives to market, including a previous One Touch model, but the One Touch Portable's peak capacity is 4TB. Seagate backs the One Touch Portable with a two-year warranty, which is typical for an external hard drive. The drive includes the useful Seagate Toolkit software, which lets you set up incremental backups and password protection for the drive, though it lacks hardware-based encryption. Also included is a two-year subscription to Rescue Data Recovery Services. We test external platter hard drives using PC Labs' external-storage testbed, a Windows desktop PC built on an Asus Prime X299 Deluxe motherboard, an Intel Core i9-10980XE Extreme Edition CPU, and an Nvidia GeForce graphics card. We also run two Mac-based tests, using a recent Apple MacBook Pro. I subjected the One Touch Portable to PC Labs' usual suite of external-storage benchmarks, comprising Crystal DiskMark 6.0, the PCMark 10 data drive benchmark, the 3DMark Storage gaming test, Blackmagic's Disk Speed Test, and our homebrew file-transfer test. The One Touch Portable comes formatted in exFAT, which ensures compatibility with macOS, Windows, and Linux computers as well as most mobile devices and gaming consoles. To test the One Touch Portable, I ran the two Mac-based tests (Blackmagic and the folder transfer speed test) first, reformatted the drive to the primarily Windows-centric NTFS, and then ran Crystal DiskMark, PCMark 10, and 3DMark Storage. The One Touch Portable proved fast for a portable hard drive on the Crystal DiskMark sequential read and write benchmarks, tallying our highest score among the small-format hard drives on the write portion of the test, and with a second-place sequential read score just short of the LaCie Mobile Drive. Both of the Seagate large-format 8TB hard drives, the One Touch and the FireCuda X, were considerably faster than the One Touch Portable and the other 2.5-inch hard drives. Keep in mind that even the fastest hard drives are snoozy compared with the slowest SSDs. The PCMark 10 data drive test aggregates a drive's results in performing a number of everyday storage tasks. In this, the One Touch Portable tallied a mediocre score, beating the LaCie and edging the Silicon Power Armor A66 but significantly lagging behind the three aforementioned WD/SanDisk 6TB hard drives as well as the 8TB Seagate One Touch and FireCuda X Vault. Hard drives, in general, are poor choices for loading or running AAA games, and the One Touch Portable is no outlier. In the 3DMark Storage test, a benchmark that aggregates a drive's performance in a number of gaming-related tasks, the One Touch Portable had the lowest score in our comparison group. The One Touch Portable did much better in the Mac-based Blackmagic disk write and read throughput tests, which measure a drive's speed in handling a range of video file formats. It had the best write and read scores among our 2.5-inch comparison hard drives. Seagate One Touch Portable (4TB) - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. In these days of through-the-roof storage prices, the introduction of a relatively portable hard drive is a welcome event, and in that role the Seagate One Touch Portable does not disappoint. For most purposes, the 4TB version we reviewed is snappy enough for a small-format hard drive, and comes with the useful Seagate Toolkit suite, which includes backup software and password protection. One downside of the One Touch Portable is its relatively low maximum capacity. Other Seagate portable hard drives have maxed out at 5TB, and several WD/SanDisk models are available at 6TB, including two Editors' Choice winners: the WD My Passport Ultra and WD My Passport, Works with USB-C. That said, why not buy multiple One Touch Portables? The relatively slow speed of hard drives makes them best for low-impact tasks and for archiving. You could, for example, use one to store photos, another for videos, and a third to house a game library. The combined cost would still be modest compared with what you'd spend on external SSDs of equivalent capacity, so the One Touch Portable is a capable contender. Since 2004, I have worked on PCMag’s hardware team, covering at various times printers, scanners, projectors, storage, and monitors. I currently focus my efforts on 3D printers, pro and productivity displays, and drives and SSDs of all sorts. Over the years, I have reviewed smart telescopes, iPad and iPhone science apps, plus the occasional camera, laptop, keyboard, and mouse. I've also written a host of articles about astronomy, space science, travel photography, and astrophotography for PCMag and its past and present sibling publications (among them, Mashable and ExtremeTech), as well as for the former PCMag Digital Edition.

item.title: SALES: The one Starlink perk that gives it an edge over traditional internet
item.description:
Source: Engadget
The one Starlink perk that gives it an edge over traditional internet Why satellite internet has a unique advantage over terrestrial providers. It's debatable as to whether Starlink markets its services properly. Anyone who's seen some of the company's ads probably understands the basics, namely that, regardless of which Starlink setup you think best suits you, you're getting the internet via a satellite dish instead of a cable or phone line. Also, if you choose the right plan, like one of the wildly different $55 plans, you can get internet access virtually anywhere in the world. However, until you dig a little deeper, many details remain mysterious, such as important specs like expected speed. One of those gaps is why you might want satellite internet when you're not roaming or otherwise isolated. In a country like the US, UK or Canada, it's rare to find a community that doesn't have at least some basic landline option. Given that Starlink can get quite expensive with its equipment costs, there has to be serious incentive to sign up. For some consumers, there is, and it's an adaptability that traditional internet lacks. It's baked into the nature of Starlink, and it could save your bacon if you value resiliency over raw speed. There are some important exceptions, which we'll get into. Why adaptability can be Starlink's big selling point Starlink's network is based around clusters of small satellites inserted into low Earth orbit (LEO). As of October 2026, there were over 11,000 working satellites, flying at altitudes ranging from about 205 to 311 miles (330 to nearly 500 kilometers). SpaceX continues to launch more, whether to expand the network or replace malfunctioning units. Essentially, there should always be a cluster overhead at any given time. The most obvious advantage of this is that whereas traditional internet connections can be knocked offline for hours by a single cable or server going down, it's rare for Starlink to suffer a similar fate. If one satellite fails, another in the same cluster should be able to pick up the slack. Even sightline obstacles aren't necessarily an issue, since the cluster approach means there's almost always a satellite with a viable angle as long as your dish is positioned properly. As mentioned, this coverage is only slated to get better. SpaceX recently filed an application with the US Federal Communications Commission to operate up to 100,000 of its Gen3 satellites, following up on a recent approval to expand Gen2 numbers as high as 15,000. If you can afford to install and maintain a dish, your internet access could hypothetically become bulletproof, short of power outages or other rare disruptions. On paper, Starlink dishes should be extremely resilient. Current-generation models can melt snow and endure temperatures from -40 to 110 degrees Fahrenheit (-40 to 43 degrees Celsius). Properly mounted, they can supposedly withstand heavy rain and winds in excess of 99 miles per hour (about 160 kilometers per hour). In practice, things don't always work perfectly. Snow takes time to melt, and there are regular, brief disruptions while your dish switches from one satellite to another. The possibility of prolonged outages remains, whether because of extreme weather, some systemic problem on Starlink's end or issues with the rest of the internet. It hardly matters how many satellites are in the sky if a particular trunk of the internet is having trouble with its local ground-based infrastructure. Some prospective users may want to actively avoid Starlink altogether. Apart from the many controversies involving founder Elon Musk, those momentary signal blips can be terrible for real-time activities like online gaming. In a shooter like Fortnite or Counter-Strike, a split second can mean the difference between landing a headshot or taking one.

item.title: SALES: The 20 highest-grossing concert films of all time
item.description:
Source: Business Insider
Concert documentaries can be a win-win for fans: they can relive favorite concerts or experience tours they couldn't see live on the big screen. The music documentary subgenre rose in popularity between 2008 and 2013, when artists such as Miley Cyrus, Michael Jackson, Justin Bieber, Katy Perry, and One Direction released major theatrical concert films to much fanfare at the box office. Ten of the 20 highest-grossing concert films on this list were released during that period, collectively earning about $318 million at the domestic box office, according to Box Office Mojo data. This type of docufilm saw a surge in the early 2020s, and in a 2024 Fandango survey, 77% of ticket buyers who had watched a concert film in 2023 said they wanted to see another tour on the silver screen. In 2023, Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour became the highest-grossing concert film of all time, with more than $180 million in domestic ticket sales. That's more than double the No. 2 entry. The release of concert documentaries has continued, with over a dozen since 2023 from artists including Billie Eilish, Beyoncé, BTS, and more. A Harry Styles tour documentary directed by John Wilson is in the works. Here are the 20 highest-grossing concert film documentaries at the domestic box office, per Box Office Mojo. 20. Amazing Grace (2018) The documentary captures Aretha Franklin recording her landmark 1972 live gospel album, "Amazing Grace," over two nights at Los Angeles' New Temple Missionary Baptist Church. The film centers on Franklin's performances with the Southern California Community Choir. 19. Bring the Soul: The Movie (2019) The documentary, directed by Park Jun-soo, BTS' primary director, centers on the band's 2018 "Love Yourself" world tour. It shows behind-the-scenes glances at each band member's life outside of the band, including the emotional and mental weight that has come with their new fame. 18. Shine a Light (2008) Academy Award-winning director Martin Scorsese films the Rolling Stones over two concerts at New York City's Beacon Theatre in 2006. The documentary centers on the band's live performance while also including archival footage and guest appearances by Buddy Guy, Christina Aguilera, and Jack White. 17. Justin Bieber's Believe (2013) Directed by Jon M. Chu, who also directed "Never Say Never," the documentary offers a behind-the-scenes and onstage look at Bieber during his 2013 "Believe" tour. It follows the pop star as he performs for packed arenas while navigating fame and the challenges of his growing career. Directed by award-winning filmmakers Paul Dugdale and Farah Khalid, the theatrical music film follows the K-pop group's sold-out performances at the SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles in 2025. It combines concert footage and behind-the-scenes content. 15. BTS: Yet to Come in Cinemas (2023) Directed by Oh Yoon-dong, the documentary features footage from the band's October 15, 2022, concert in Busan, South Korea. The free Busan concert supported the city's bid to host the 2030 World Expo and was BTS's last performance with all seven members before military enlistments began. 14. U2: Rattle and Hum (1988) Director Phil Joanou's documentary follows U2 during its "The Joshua Tree" tour, as the band sought to connect more with American blues, gospel, folk, and rock music. It includes live performances, studio sessions, and scenes of Bono and his bandmates recording with artists such as B.B. King. 13. Billie Eilish: Hit Me Hard and Soft (2026) Co-directed by Billie Eilish and James Cameron, the 3D concert film captures Eilish's sold-out "Hit Me Hard and Soft" world tour. It features performances of songs from the album, including "Birds of a Feather" and "Wildflower," alongside backstage footage of Eilish, her brother and collaborator Finneas, her band, and the production team behind the tour. 12. Stop Making Sense (1984) Jonathan Demme's film documents Talking Heads' 1983 concerts at the Pantages Theatre in Hollywood. The performance begins with David Byrne alone onstage and gradually expands, song by song, as musicians, backing singers, props, and Byrne's famously oversized suit transform the stage into a full production. 11. U2 3D (2008) Directed by Catherine Owens and Mark Pellington, the documentary was filmed during the band's Vertigo Tour in South America. It uses 3D filming technology to highlight the scale of U2's stadium show, including the massive video screens and the crowd's response. 10. Glee: The 3D Concert Movie (2011) This documentary, directed by Kevin Tancharoen, captures the cast of "Glee" performing songs from the series during its live concert tour. 9. Madonna: Truth or Dare (1991) Alek Keshishian's documentary follows Madonna during her 1990 Blond Ambition Tour, one of the most controversial pop tours of its era due to it blending R-rated choreography with religious symbols. Color concert footage is set against black-and-white scenes of Madonna rehearsing, traveling, meeting with family, and speaking candidly with her dancers and entourage. 8. Jonas Brothers: The 3D Concert Experience (2009) The Jonas Brothers' 2008 "Burning Up" tour is the focus of this concert film. Directed by Bruce Hendricks, it was filmed largely at the Honda Center in Anaheim. 7. Katy Perry: Part of Me (2012) Directed by Dan Cutforth and Jane Lipsitz, the 3D documentary follows Katy Perry during her California Dreams Tour. 6. One Direction: This Is Us (2013) Morgan Spurlock's documentary follows One Direction as it tours stadiums while navigating fame. The film looks back at how the band was assembled on "The X Factor," while also showing their family lives and life on the road. 5. Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé (2023) Written, directed, and produced by Beyoncé, the documentary follows the creation and 2023 run of her Renaissance World Tour. It combines concert footage from the stadium production with behind-the-scenes scenes of Beyoncé working with her dancers, family, crew, and creative team. 4. Hannah Montana and Miley Cyrus: Best of Both Worlds Concert (2008) This concert documentary follows Miley Cyrus on her 2007 and 2008 "Best of Both Worlds" tour, when she performed as both herself and her Disney Channel character, Hannah Montana. Directed by Bruce Hendricks, it includes concert performances, backstage moments, and appearances by the Jonas Brothers. 3. This Is It (2009) Director Kenny Ortega assembled this documentary from rehearsal footage for Michael Jackson's planned "This Is It" residency at London's O2 Arena. Rather than showing the completed concert, it shows Jackson in the final months of his life rehearsing songs, directing dancers, revising musical arrangements, and planning production. 2. Justin Bieber: Never Say Never (2011) Director Jon M. Chu follows Justin Bieber's path from uploading covers on YouTube to becoming a teenage pop star. It builds toward his sold-out Madison Square Garden show, while also including interviews with his mother, manager Scooter Braun, Usher, and fans. 1. Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour (2023) Directed by Sam Wrench, who also directed Billie Eilish's 2023 documentary, the film documents Swift's 2023 Eras Tour concerts at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles. It shows the Taylor Swift's career-spanning set list, along with the costumes, choreography, dancers, screens, and stage effects behind each concert.
